background: Graph Steiner tree asks for the cheapest connected subgraph spanning a specified terminal set and is a foundational network-design problem. The approximation landscape has an unusually large gap: sophisticated LP rounding gives a ratio of $\ln 4\approx1.386$, while NP-hardness only rules out ratios below $96/95$. The best algorithm uses the hypergraphic relaxation and iterative randomized rounding, which captures full components connecting terminals through Steiner vertices. Despite the strength of this relaxation, known lower bounds for its integrality gap are much smaller than $\ln4$. The open problem is therefore both algorithmic and polyhedral: identify the true approximation threshold for Steiner tree and the true power of the hypergraphic LP.
full_statement: In the graph Steiner tree problem, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge costs and a terminal set $R\subseteq V$. The goal is to find a minimum-cost connected subgraph spanning all terminals; nonterminals may be used as Steiner vertices. Let $\alpha^*$ be the best polynomial-time approximation ratio achievable for general graph Steiner tree, assuming $P\ne NP$. Let $\gamma_{\mathrm{hyp}}$ be the integrality gap of the hypergraphic relaxation, whose variables correspond to full components connecting subsets of terminals and whose constraints encode terminal connectivity. Determine $\alpha^*$ and $\gamma_{\mathrm{hyp}}$, or at least close the current gap between the best algorithmic guarantee $\ln4+\epsilon$, the best known hypergraphic-LP lower bound around $8/7$, and the best NP-hardness threshold $96/95$. A solution should specify whether the hypergraphic LP is the right barrier or whether stronger algorithms/hardness reductions move the true threshold elsewhere.
open_problem: Determine the optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for graph Steiner tree and the exact integrality gap of the hypergraphic relaxation.
known_results: Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoss, and Sanita give a $(\ln4+\epsilon)$-approximation via iterative randomized rounding of the hypergraphic relaxation, and Goemans, Olver, Rothvoss, and Zenklusen later gave a deterministic analysis proving a matching $\ln4$ upper bound on the hypergraphic integrality gap. Chlebik and Chlebikova prove NP-hardness of approximation below $96/95$. Known lower-bound instances for the hypergraphic relaxation give a gap at least $8/7$, far below $\ln4$. Recent work has improved the related bidirected-cut relaxation below $2$, but that does not resolve the stronger hypergraphic relaxation or the true approximation threshold. Thus algorithmic, LP-gap, and hardness bounds remain widely separated.

where_posed.text: Gap left by Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoss, and Sanita's hypergraphic-LP algorithm and Chlebik-Chlebikova hardness.

progress.summary: Best algorithm is $\ln4+\epsilon$; best hardness is $96/95$; hypergraphic-LP gap is between $8/7$ and $\ln4$.

links.title: Byrka et al., iterative randomized rounding

counterexample_rationale: Integrality-gap lower bounds are explicit finite Steiner instances. Approximation hardness requires reductions, but finite LP gaps are searchable and checkable.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over terminal/Steiner graph gadgets can find stronger hypergraphic-LP gaps or identify families where known rounding is loose.

literature.synthesis: The hypergraphic relaxation was a major advance because it reasons about full components rather than individual edges, enabling iterative randomized rounding below earlier combinatorial ratios. The remaining gap may be due to a loose analysis of that rounding, an actual gap in the relaxation, or a much stronger hardness construction still unknown. Bidirected-cut developments are related but not identical: BCR is compact and practical, while hypergraphic relaxations are stronger but component-heavy. A resolution likely needs either a new rounding theorem for components or a better understanding of hard instances for terminal-connectivity relaxations.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Search for hypergraphic-relaxation gap instances and compare them to BCR gaps. Algorithmic attacks should inspect where iterative randomized rounding loses the $\ln4$ factor.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Distinguish graph Steiner tree from Euclidean Steiner tree, prize-collecting Steiner tree, and Steiner forest. A hypergraphic-LP gap claim must specify the exact relaxation, including whether all full components are allowed or only bounded-size components, and must certify both the LP value and the optimum Steiner tree cost. A claimed approximation improvement must run in polynomial time for arbitrary graph instances and cannot rely on a fixed number of terminals unless stated as a parameterized result.
